questions.question: All the four entries of the \(2 \times 2\) matrix \[{P} = \begin{bmatrix} p_{11} & p_{12} \\ p_{21} & p_{22} \end{bmatrix}\] are nonzero, and one of its eigenvalues is zero. Which of the following statements is true?
questions.explanation: Given the \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(P\): \[P = \begin{bmatrix} P_{11} & P_{12} \\ P_{21} & P_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \text{ where } P_{ij} \neq 0 \quad \forall \,\, i,j\] It is stated that one of the eigenvalues of matrix \(P\) is zero. Let the eigenvalues be \(\lambda_{1}\) and \(\lambda_{2}\). If \(\lambda_{1} = 0\), then: \[\lambda_{1} \cdot \lambda_{2} = \text{Det}(P)\] \[0 \cdot \lambda_{2} = \text{Det}(P) \implies \text{Det}(P) = 0\] A matrix with a zero determinant is a singular matrix. For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, the determinant is calculated as: \[|P| = P_{11}P_{22} - P_{12}P_{21}\] \[P_{11}P_{22} - P_{12}P_{21} = 0\] Thus, option (C) is correct. \[\boxed{\text{(C) $p_{11}p_{22} - p_{12}p_{21} = 0$}}\]

questions.question: For real values of \(x\), the minimum value of function \(f(x) = e^x + e^{-x}\) is
questions.explanation: Given function: \[f(x) = e^x + e^{-x}, \quad \text{where } x \in \mathbb{R}\] First, find the first and second derivatives of the function with respect to \(x\): \[f'(x) = e^x - e^{-x}\] \[f''(x) = e^x + e^{-x}\] For locating stationary points, set the first derivative to zero: \[f'(x) = 0 \implies e^x - e^{-x} = 0\] \[e^x = e^{-x}\] Multiplying both sides by \(e^x\): \[e^{2x} = 1\] Taking the natural logarithm on both sides: \[\ln(e^{2x}) = \ln(1)\] \[2x = 0 \implies x = 0\] Thus, \(x = 0\) is the stationary point. Test the stationary point using the second derivative: \[f''(0) = e^0 + e^{-0} = 1 + 1 = 2 > 0\] Since \(f''(0) > 0\), the function \(f(x)\) achieves a local minimum value at \(x = 0\). The corresponding minimum value of the function is: \[f(0) = e^0 + e^{-0} = 1 + 1 = 2\] Hence, the correct option is (a). \[\boxed{\text{(a)}\ \ 2}\]

questions.question: Which of the following function would have only odd powers of \(x\) in its Taylor series expansion about the point \(x = 0\)?
questions.explanation: The standard Maclaurin series expansion for \(\sin \theta\) is given by: \[\sin \theta = \theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!} - \dots\] To find the series expansion for \(\sin x^3\), substitute \(\theta = x^3\) into the expansion: \[\sin x^3 = (x^3) - \frac{(x^3)^3}{3!} + \frac{(x^3)^5}{5!} - \dots\] \[\sin x^3 = x^3 - \frac{x^9}{3!} + \frac{x^{15}}{5!} - \dots\] Hence, the correct option is (a). \[\boxed{\text{(a)}\ \ \sin(x^3)}\]

questions.question: In the Taylor series expansion of \(e^x + \sin x\) about the point \(x = \pi\), the coefficient of \((x - \pi)^2\) is
questions.explanation: Given function: \[f(x) = e^x + \sin x\] Compute the values of the function and its derivatives evaluated at \(x = \pi\): \[f(\pi) = e^{\pi} + \sin \pi = e^{\pi} + 0 = e^{\pi}\] \[f'(x) = e^x + \cos x \implies f'(\pi) = e^{\pi} + \cos \pi = e^{\pi} - 1\] \[f''(x) = e^x - \sin x \implies f''(\pi) = e^{\pi} - \sin \pi = e^{\pi}\] The Taylor series expansion of a function \(f(x)\) about the point \(x = \pi\) is defined as: \[f(x) = f(\pi) + (x - \pi)f'(\pi) + \frac{(x - \pi)^2}{2!}f''(\pi) + \dots\] The coefficient belonging to the term \((x - \pi)^2\) is: \[\text{Coefficient} = \frac{f''(\pi)}{2!} = \frac{e^{\pi}}{2}\] Hence, the correct option is (b). \[\boxed{\text{(b)}\ \ \frac{e^{\pi}}{2}}\]

questions.question: The value of the integral of the function \(g(x,y) = 4x^3 + 10y^4\) along the straight line segment from the point \((0, 0)\) to the point \((1, 2)\) in the \(xy\)-plane is
questions.explanation: Given function: \[g(x, y) = 4x^3 + 10y^4\] The path of integration is a straight line segment connecting \((0, 0)\) to \((1, 2)\). The equation of this straight line segment is: \[y = 2x \implies dy = 2 \, dx\] As the path goes from \((0,0)\) to \((1,2)\), the variable \(x\) ranges from \(0\) to \(1\). The line integral of the function \(g(x, y)\) along this path \(C\) with respect to \(x\) is: \[\int_{C} g(x, y) \, dx = \int_{0}^{1} \left[ 4x^3 + 10(2x)^4 \right] \, dx\] \[= \int_{0}^{1} \left[ 4x^3 + 10(16x^4) \right] \, dx\] \[= \int_{0}^{1} \left[ 4x^3 + 160x^4 \right] \, dx\] Evaluating the definite integral: \[= \left[ 4 \cdot \frac{x^4}{4} + 160 \cdot \frac{x^5}{5} \right]_{0}^{1}\] \[= \left[ x^4 + 32x^5 \right]_{0}^{1}\] \[= (1^4 + 32 \cdot 1^5) - (0 + 0)\] \[= 1 + 32 = 33\] Hence, the correct option is (a). \[\boxed{\text{(a)}\ \ 33}\]

questions.question: Consider points \(P\) and \(Q\) in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane, with \(P=(1,0)\) and \(Q=(0,1)\). The line integral \[2\int_P^Q (x\,dx+y\,dy)\] along the semicircle with the line segment \(PQ\) as its diameter
options: depends on the direction (clockwise or anti-clockwise) of the semicircle
questions.explanation:
Given, \[P=(1,0), \qquad Q=(0,1)\] We need to evaluate \[2\int_{P}^{Q} (x\,dx+y\,dy)\] along the semicircular path having \(PQ\) as diameter.
Method 1
Observe that \[x\,dx+y\,dy = \frac{1}{2}d(x^{2}+y^{2})\] Therefore, \[2\int_{P}^{Q} (x\,dx+y\,dy) = \int_{P}^{Q} d(x^{2}+y^{2})\] Using the fundamental theorem for line integrals, \[= \left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)_{Q} - \left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)_{P}\] At point \(Q=(0,1)\), \[x^{2}+y^{2}=0^{2}+1^{2}=1\] At point \(P=(1,0)\), \[x^{2}+y^{2}=1^{2}+0^{2}=1\] Hence, \[2\int_{P}^{Q} (x\,dx+y\,dy) = 1-1 = 0\]
Method 2
Since the variables of integration match the terms, integrate separately: \[2\int_{P}^{Q} (x\,dx+y\,dy) = 2\int_{P}^{Q} x\,dx + 2\int_{P}^{Q} y\,dy\] Now, \[2\int x\,dx = x^2\] and \[2\int y\,dy = y^2\] Therefore, \[2\int_{P}^{Q} (x\,dx+y\,dy) = \left[x^2+y^2\right]_{P}^{Q}\] At \(Q=(0,1)\), \[x^2+y^2 = 0^2+1^2 = 1\] At \(P=(1,0)\), \[x^2+y^2 = 1^2+0^2 = 1\] Hence, \[2\int_{P}^{Q} (x\,dx+y\,dy) = 1-1 = 0\]
\[\boxed{\text{(b) }0}\]
Key points
  • The integrand is an exact differential: \[d(x^{2}+y^{2})=2x\,dx+2y\,dy\]
  • Line integrals of conservative vector fields are path independent.
  • Only the initial and final points are needed for evaluation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a solution of the differential equation \(\dfrac{dx(t)}{dt}+3x(t)=0\) with initial condition x(0)=2?
questions.explanation:
Given differential equation is \[\frac{dx(t)}{dt}+3x(t) = 0\ \ \text{with initial condition}\ \ x(0) = 2\]
Method 1
Separating variables & Integrating both sides, \[\int \frac{dx}{x} = -3\int dt\] \[\ln x = -3t + C\] \[x = Ce^{-3t}\] Using the initial condition \(x(0)=2\), \[2 = Ce^{0} \Rightarrow\ C = 2\] Hence, \[x(t) = 2e^{-3t}\]
Method 2
Replacing \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\) by \(D\), \[(D+3)x = 0\] The auxiliary equation is \[m + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow\ m = -3\] Therefore, the complementary function is \[x(t) = Ce^{-3t}\] Using \(x(0) = 2, C = 2\) Hence, \[x(t) = 2e^{-3t}\]
Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\ x(t) = 2e^{-3t}}\]

questions.question: The equation \(\sin(z) = 10\) has
options: an infinite number of complex solutions
questions.explanation: \[\sin(z) = 10\] \[\frac{\text{e}^{\text{j}z} - \text{e}^{-\text{j}z}}{2\text{j}} = 10\] \[\text{e}^{2\text{j}z} - \text{j}20\text{e}^{\text{j}z} - 1 = 0\] \[\text{e}^{\text{j}z} = \frac{\text{j}20 \pm \sqrt{-400 + 4}}{2} = \frac{\text{j}20 \pm 6\text{j}\sqrt{11}}{2} = 10\text{j} \pm 3\text{j}\sqrt{11}\] \[\text{j}z = \ln\left[ 10\text{j} \pm 3\text{j}\sqrt{11} \right] = \ln\text{j} + \ln\left[ 10 \pm 3\sqrt{11} \right]\] \[\text{j}z = \ln\text{e}^{\text{j}\frac{\pi}{2} \pm 2\text{n}\pi} + \ln\left[ 10 \pm 3\sqrt{11} \right]\] \[\text{j}z = \text{j}\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \pm 2\text{n}\pi \right) + \ln\left[ 10 \pm 3\sqrt{11} \right]\] Hence this equation has infinite number of complex solutions. \[\boxed{D. \text{an infinite number of complex solutions}}\]

questions.question: \(P_X(x) = M e^{-2\lvert x \rvert}\ + N e^{-3\lvert x \rvert}\) is the probability density function for the real random variable \(X\), over the entire \(x\) axis. \(M\) and \(N\) are both positive real numbers. The equation relating \(M\) and \(N\) is
questions.explanation:
Since \(P_X(x)\) is a probability density function over the entire real axis, \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} P_X(x)\,dx=1\] Given, \[P_X(x)=Me^{-2|x|}+Ne^{-3|x|}\] Therefore, \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(Me^{-2|x|}+Ne^{-3|x|}\right)dx=1\] Using \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-a|x|}\,dx=\frac{2}{a}\] we get \[M\left(\frac{2}{2}\right)+N\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)=1\] \[M+\frac{2}{3}N=1\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) } M+\frac{2}{3}N=1}\]
Key points
  • Total probability for a pdf over entire real line is \(1\).
  • Standard result: \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-a|x|}\,dx=\frac{2}{a}\]

questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure is used to charge the capacitor \(C\) alternately from two current sources as indicated. The switches \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are mechanically coupled and connected as follows : For \(2nT \le t < (2n+1)T\), \((n = 0, 1, 2, \dots)\) \(S_1\) to \(P_1\) and \(S_2\) to \(P_2\) For \((2n+1)T \le t < (2n+2)T\), \((n = 0, 1, 2, \dots)\) \(S_1\) to \(Q_1\) and \(S_2\) to \(Q_2\). Assume that the capacitor has zero initial charge. Given that \(u(t)\) is a unit step function, the voltage \(V_C(t)\) across the capacitor is given by
questions.explanation:
Given, \(Q(0^-)=0~\text{C}\), \[V_C(0^-) = \dfrac{Q(0^-)}{C} \ \Rightarrow \ V_C(0^-)=0~\text{V}\] From the property of capacitor, \[V_C(0^-)=V_C(0^+)=0~\text{V}\] The switching sequence is
\(n\)\(t\)Position of \(S_1\)Position of \(S_2\)
0\(0\le t<T\)\(S_1\rightarrow P_1\)\(S_2\rightarrow P_2\)
0\(T\le t<2T\)\(S_1\rightarrow Q_1\)\(S_2\rightarrow Q_2\)
1\(2T\le t<3T\)\(S_1\rightarrow P_1\)\(S_2\rightarrow P_2\)
1\(3T\le t<4T\)\(S_1\rightarrow Q_1\)\(S_2\rightarrow Q_2\)
2\(4T\le t<5T\)\(S_1\rightarrow P_1\)\(S_2\rightarrow P_2\)
2\(5T\le t<6T\)\(S_1\rightarrow Q_1\)\(S_2\rightarrow Q_2\)
Case 1:
When \(S_1\) is connected to \(P_1\) and \(S_2\) is connected to \(P_2\), For \(n=0\), \(0\le t<T\) \[i_C(t)=1~\text{A}=u(t)\] The capacitor voltage is \[V_C(t) = \frac{1}{C} \int_{-\infty}^{t}i_C(\tau)\,d\tau= V_C(0^-) + \frac{1}{C} \int_0^t i_C(\tau)\,d\tau\] \[\because V_C(0)=0, \qquad C=1~\text{F}\] \[V_C(t) = 0 + \int_0^t1\,dt =t\] This graph indicates the linear charging of the capacitor as a constant current flows through the capacitor. Case 2:
Similarly, when \(S_1\) is connected to \(Q_1\) and \(S_2\) is connected to \(Q_2\), For \(n=0\), \(T\le t<2T\) \[i_C(t)=-1~\text{A}=-u(t)\] The capacitor voltage is \[V_C(t) = \frac{1}{C} \int_{-\infty}^{0}i_C(t)\,dt + \frac{1}{C} \int_{0}^{T}i_C(t)\,dt + \frac{1}{C} \int_{T}^{t}i_C(t)\,dt\] Since \(C=1~\text{F}\), \[V_C(t) = 0 + T + \int_{T}^{t}(-1)\,dtV_C(t) = 0+T-\int_{T}^{t}1\,dt\] \[V_C(t) = T-(t-T) = 2T-t\] This graph indicates the linear discharging of the capacitor as a constant current flows through the capacitor. Combining both the cases together, So; Using unit step functions, \[V_C(t) = tu(t) - (t-T)u(t-T) - (t-T)u(t-T) + (t-2T)u(t-2T)+...\] \[= tu(t) - 2(t-T)u(t-T) + 2(t-2T)u(t-2T)\] \[\qquad -(t-3T)u(t-3T) -(t-3T)u(t-3T) +\cdots\] \[V_C(t) = tu(t) + 2 \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^n (t-nT)\, u(t-nT)\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }\; tu(t) + 2 \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^n (t-nT)\, u(t-nT)}\]

questions.question: In the following circuit, the switch \(S\) is closed at \(t = 0\). The rate of change of current \(\dfrac{di}{dt}(0^+)\) is given by
questions.explanation: The current through the inductor is given by, \(i(t) = i(\infty) + \left[i(0^+)-i(\infty)\right]e^{-t/\tau}\) At \(t=0^-\), the switch is open and the circuit is in steady state. Hence, the inductor behaves as a short circuit. Therefore, \(i(0^-)=0\) \(\Rightarrow \ i(0^-)=i(0^+)=0\) For the RL network, \(\tau = \dfrac{L}{R_{\mathrm{th}}}\) where, \(R_{\mathrm{th}}\) is the Thevenin resistance seen by the inductor when the current source is open-circuited. From the figure, \(R_{\mathrm{th}} = R+R_s\) Hence, \[\tau = \frac{L}{R+R_s}\] At \(t=\infty\), the inductor behaves as a short circuit. Applying KVL, \[-\left[I_s-i(\infty)\right]R_s + Ri(\infty) = 0\] \[i(\infty)(R+R_s) = I_sR_s\] \[i(\infty) = \frac{I_sR_s}{R+R_s}\] Substituting the values, \[i(t) = \frac{I_sR_s}{R+R_s} \left[ 1-e^{-(R+R_s)t/L} \right]\] \[\frac{di(t)}{dt} = \frac{I_sR_s}{R+R_s} \left[ e^{-(R+R_s)t/L} \times \frac{R+R_s}{L} \right], \qquad \text{[Differentiating]}\] At \(t=0^+\), \[\left.\frac{di(t)}{dt}\right|_{0^+} = \frac{I_sR_s}{L}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\dfrac{R_sI_s}{L}}\]

When \(S_1\) is open and \(S_2\) is closed \[V_1 = h_{11}I_1 + h_{12}V_2\] \[4.5 = h_{12} \times 1.5 \,\text{[Since $I_1$ is 0A]}\] \[\therefore h_{12} = 3\] \(I_2 = h_{21}I_1 + h_{22}V_2\) Similarly \[1 = h_{22} \times 1.5\] \[h_{22} = \frac{2}{3} = 0.67\] When \(S_1\) is closed and \(S_2\) is open \[V_1 = h_{11}I_1 + h_{12}V_2\] \[6 = h_{11} \times 4 + 3 \times 6\] \[h_{11} = -3\] Similarly \(I_2 = h_{21}I_1 + h_{22}V_2\) \[0 = h_{21} \times 4 + h_{22} \times 6\] \[h_{21} = -1\] Thus we can form the matrix as : \[H = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 3 \\ -1 & 0.67 \end{bmatrix}\]
Method 2
We have the z-parameter matrix as : \[Z = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & 4.5 \\ 1.5 & 1.5 \end{bmatrix}\] From this we can write:- \[V_1 = 1.5I_1 + 4.5I_2 \quad - (1)\] \[V_2 = 1.5I_1 + 1.5I_2 \quad - (2)\] From (2), \[I_2 = \frac{V_2}{1.5} - I_1 \quad - (3) \qquad \text{Thus } h_{21} = -1 \text{ and } h_{22} = 0.67\] Putting (3) in (1) \[V_1 = 1.5I_1 + 4.5\left(\frac{V_2}{1.5} - I_1\right)\] \[= -3I_1 + 3V_2\] Thus \(h_{11} = -3\) and \(h_{12} = 3\). Hence we write the matrix as:- \[H = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 3 \\ -1 & 0.67 \end{bmatrix}\]
Key points
  • Here the polarity of ammeter \(I_2\) is such that it measures direction of current going inwards into the 2 port network to be positive, which is the conventional direction of \(I_2\) in standard 2 port parameters. However, it must be noted that in case the ammeter polarity was marked to be opposite, a suitable adjustment had to be made (taking \(-I_2\) in calculations).
\[\boxed{(a)\begin{bmatrix}-3&3\\-1&0.67\end{bmatrix}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The input and output of a continuous time system are respectively denoted by \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\). Which of the following descriptions corresponds to a causal system?
questions.explanation:
A continuous-time system is causal if its output \(y(t)\) at any given time \(t\) depends only on the present and past values of the input \(x(t)\). It must not depend on future values of the input (i.e., \(x(t+\tau)\) where \(\tau > 0\)). Let us analyze the dependence of \(y(t)\) on \(x(t)\) for each option:
  • Option (A):
    \[y(t) = x(t - 2) + x(t + 4)\] The term \(x(t + 4)\) represents a future input (e.g., at \(t=0\), the output \(y(0)\) depends on \(x(4)\)). Thus, the system is non-causal.
  • Option (B):
    \[y(t) = (t - 4)x(t + 1)\] The term \(x(t + 1)\) depends on a future input. Thus, the system is non-causal.
  • Option (C):
    \[y(t) = (t + 4)x(t - 1)\] The term \(x(t - 1)\) depends only on a past input for any given \(t\). The coefficient \((t + 4)\) is a time-varying gain and does not affect the causality of the system. Thus, the system is causal.
  • Option (D):
    \[y(t) = (t + 5)x(t + 5)\] The term \(x(t + 5)\) represents a future input. Thus, the system is non-causal.
\[\boxed{\text{C) $y(t) = (t + 4)x(t - 1)$ }}\]
Key points
  • A system is causal if the output at any time \(t_0\) depends only on inputs \(x(t)\) for \(t \le t_0\).
  • Time-varying coefficients (like \(t+4\) or \(t-4\)) make a system time-varying but do not determine causality. Causality is solely dependent on the time shift of the input signal \(x(\cdot)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Confusing time-variance with non-causality. The presence of \(t\) as an external multiplier has no bearing on whether the system requires future inputs.
  • Misinterpreting the sign inside the function argument. For \(\tau > 0\), \(x(t - \tau)\) represents a delay (past, causal) while \(x(t + \tau)\) represents an advance (future, non-causal).

questions.question: The impulse response \(h(t)\) of a linear time invari ant continuous time system is described by \(h(t) = \exp(\alpha t)u(t) + \exp(\beta t)u(-t)\), where \(u(-t)\) denotes the unit step function, and \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are real constants. This system is stable if
questions.explanation:
For the given LTI system, the impulse response is \(h(t) = h_{1}(t) + h_{2}(t)\). Where \(h_{1}(t) = e^{\alpha t} u(t)\) is shown in Fig. 1 for \(\alpha < 0\) and \(h_{2}(t) = e^{\beta t} u(-t)\) is shown in Fig. 2 for \(\beta > 0\). For stability of LTI system \[I = \int_{t=-\infty}^{\infty} \left|h(t)\right|\,dt < \infty\] \[I_{1} = \int_{t=0}^{\infty} e^{\alpha t}\,dt = \frac{1}{|\alpha|} = \text{constant} (< \infty)\] \[I_{2} = \int_{t=-\infty}^{0} e^{\beta t}\,dt = \frac{1}{\beta} = \text{constant} (< \infty)\] \[I = I_{1} + I_{2} = \text{constant} (< \infty)\] \[\boxed{\text{D) $\alpha$ is negative and $\beta$ is positive }}\]
Key points
  • An LTI system is Bounded-Input Bounded-Output (BIBO) stable if and only if its impulse response \(h(t)\) is absolutely integrable: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |h(t)|\,dt < \infty\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question:
Let \(x(t)\) be the input and \(y(t)\) be the output of a con tinuous time system. Match the system properties P1, P2 and P3 with system relations R1, R2, R3, R4.
PropertiesRelations
P1: Linear but NOT time-invariantR1: \(y(t) = t^2x(t)\)
P2: Time-invariant but NOT linearR2 : \(y(t) = t|x(t)|\)
P3: Linear and time-invariantR3 : \(y(t) = |x(t)|\)
R4 : \(y(t) = x(t - 5)\)
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct mapping, we need to test each relation for the properties of linearity and time-invariance. Relation R1: \(y(t) = t^2x(t)\)
  • Linearity: Let \(x(t) = a x_1(t) + b x_2(t)\). \[y(t) = t^2(a x_1(t) + b x_2(t)) = a t^2 x_1(t) + b t^2 x_2(t) = a y_1(t) + b y_2(t)\] Since it satisfies the superposition principle, it is Linear.
  • Time-Invariance: Let the input be delayed by \(t_0\), forming \(x_1(t) = x(t-t_0)\). The response is \(y_1(t) = t^2 x(t-t_0)\). Now, delay the original output by \(t_0\): \(y(t-t_0) = (t-t_0)^2 x(t-t_0)\). Since \(y_1(t) eq y(t-t_0)\), the system is NOT time-invariant.
Conclusion for R1: Linear but NOT time-invariant (P1). Relation R2: \(y(t) = t|x(t)|\)
  • Linearity: The absolute value operator is non-linear. For a constant \(a < 0\), the response to \(a x(t)\) is \(t|a x(t)| = t|a||x(t)| eq a t|x(t)|\). Thus, it is NOT linear.
  • Time-Invariance: Due to the explicit time multiplier \(t\), applying the same shift test as in R1 will yield \(y_1(t) = t|x(t-t_0)|\) and \(y(t-t_0) = (t-t_0)|x(t-t_0)|\). It is NOT time-invariant.
Conclusion for R2: Neither linear nor time-invariant (Does not match P1, P2, or P3). Relation R3: \(y(t) = |x(t)|\)
  • Linearity: Because of the absolute value, \(|a x(t)| = |a||x(t)| eq a|x(t)|\) for \(a < 0\). It is NOT linear.
  • Time-Invariance: Let the input be delayed by \(t_0\): \(y_1(t) = |x(t-t_0)|\). Delaying the output by \(t_0\) gives \(y(t-t_0) = |x(t-t_0)|\). Since \(y_1(t) = y(t-t_0)\), the system is Time-invariant.
Conclusion for R3: Time-invariant but NOT linear (P2). Relation R4: \(y(t) = x(t-5)\)
  • Linearity: This represents a pure time delay. \(a x_1(t-5) + b x_2(t-5) = a y_1(t) + b y_2(t)\). It is Linear.
  • Time-Invariance: Delaying the input by \(t_0\) yields \(y_1(t) = x((t-t_0)-5) = x(t-t_0-5)\). Delaying the output yields \(y(t-t_0) = x((t-t_0)-5)\). Since they are equal, it is Time-invariant.
Conclusion for R4: Linear and time-invariant (P3). Matching the properties to the relations: P1 \( ightarrow\) R1 P2 \( ightarrow\) R3 P3 \( ightarrow\) R4 \[ oxed{ ext{A) (P1, R1), (P2, R3), (P3, R4) }}\]
Key points
  • Linearity Check: A system is linear if it obeys superposition: \(\mathcal{H}\{a x_1(t) + b x_2(t)\} = a \mathcal{H}\{x_1(t)\} + b \mathcal{H}\{x_2(t)\}\). Operations like absolute value \(|x(t)|\), squaring \(x^2(t)\), or adding a non-zero constant violate linearity.
  • Time-Invariance Check: A system is time-invariant if \(\mathcal{H}\{x(t-t_0)\} = y(t-t_0)\). Multiplying the input signal by explicit functions of time (like \(t\) or \(t^2\)) or time-scaling (like \(x(2t)\)) violates time-invariance.
  • Pure Delay: A pure time-shift system \(y(t) = x(t-t_d)\) is always an LTI (Linear Time-Invariant) system.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ignoring negative scalars in linearity tests: When checking absolute values or even-power functions, students often forget that linearity requires scaling to hold for all real (or complex) numbers, including negative ones. \(|-1 \cdot x(t)| eq -1 \cdot |x(t)|\).
  • Improper shift application: When checking for time-invariance, you must find the response to a delayed input \(x_1(t) = x(t-t_0)\). Do not mistakenly replace the independent variable \(t\) outside the function argument \(x(\dots)\). For \(y(t) = t^2 x(t)\), the delayed input response is \(t^2 x(t-t_0)\), not \((t-t_0)^2 x(t-t_0)\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The signal \(x(t)\) is described by \[x(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & for \ -1 \le t \le +1 \\ 0 & otherwise \end{cases}\] Two of the angular frequencies at which its Fourier transform becomes zero are
questions.explanation:
The given signal is a rectangular pulse in the time domain: \[x(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } -1 \le t \le +1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\] The Fourier transform \(X(\omega)\) of the signal \(x(t)\) is given by the definition: \[X(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) e^{-j\omega t} dt\] Substituting the given \(x(t)\): \[X(\omega) = \int_{-1}^{1} 1 \cdot e^{-j\omega t} dt = \left[ \frac{e^{-j\omega t}}{-j\omega} \right]_{-1}^{1}\] \[X(\omega) = \frac{e^{-j\omega} - e^{j\omega}}{-j\omega} = \frac{2\sin(\omega)}{\omega}\] We need to find the angular frequencies where the Fourier transform becomes zero, i.e., \(X(\omega) = 0\). \[\frac{2\sin(\omega)}{\omega} = 0\] This condition is satisfied when the numerator is zero, provided the denominator is not zero: \[\sin(\omega) = 0 \implies \omega = n\pi \quad \text{for } n = \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \dots\] Note that for \(n = 0\), \(\omega = 0\), the value is calculated using L'Hôpital's rule (or standard limits): \[\lim_{\omega \to 0} \frac{2\sin(\omega)}{\omega} = 2 \neq 0\] Thus, the angular frequencies at which the Fourier transform becomes zero are \(\pm\pi, \pm2\pi, \pm3\pi, \dots\) From the given options, \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\) are two such valid angular frequencies. \[\boxed{\text{A) $\pi, 2\pi$ }}\]
Key points
  • Fourier Transform of a Rectangular Pulse: A rectangular pulse in the time domain transforms into a sinc function (or sampling function) in the frequency domain.
  • For a rectangular pulse of total width \(\tau\) centered at the origin, the zero crossings in the frequency domain occur at integer multiples of \(\frac{2\pi}{\tau}\) (excluding zero). Here, \(\tau = 2\), so the zero crossings are at \(n\pi\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The impulse response \(h(t)\) of a linear time invariant continuous time system is given by \(h(t)=\exp(-2t)u(t)\), where \(u(t)\) denotes the unit step function The output of this system, to the sinusoidal input \(x(t)=2\cos(2t)\) for all time \(t\), is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Input: \[x(t) = 2 \cos(2t)\] Frequency response: \[X(\omega) = 2\pi[\delta(\omega - 2) + \delta(\omega + 2)]\] \[H(\omega) = \frac{1}{2 + j\omega}\] Output: \[Y(\omega) = H(\omega)X(\omega)\] \[\begin{aligned} Y(\omega) &= \frac{1}{2+j\omega} \cdot 2\pi[\delta(\omega - 2) + \delta(\omega + 2)] \\ &= \frac{2\pi}{2+j2}\delta(\omega - 2) + \frac{2\pi}{2-j2}\delta(\omega + 2) \\ &= \frac{2\pi}{8} [(2 - j2)\delta(\omega - 2) + (2 + j2)\delta(\omega + 2)] \\ &= \frac{\pi}{4} [2\{\delta(\omega - 2) + \delta(\omega + 2)\} + j2\{\delta(\omega + 2) - \delta(\omega - 2)\}] \\ &= \frac{\pi}{2}[\delta(\omega - 2) + \delta(\omega + 2)] - j\frac{\pi}{2}[\delta(\omega - 2) - \delta(\omega + 2)] \end{aligned}\] Taking the inverse Fourier transform: \[\therefore \quad y(t) = \frac{\cos 2t}{2} + \frac{\sin 2t}{2}\] \[\begin{aligned} y(t) &= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \left[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos 2t + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin 2t \right] \\ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos(2t - 0.25\pi) \\ &= 2^{-0.5} \cos(2t - 0.25\pi) \end{aligned}\]
Method 2
For a stable LTI system, the steady-state response to a sinusoidal input \(x(t) = A \cos(\omega_0 t)\) is given directly by: \[y(t) = A |H(j\omega_0)| \cos(\omega_0 t + \angle H(j\omega_0))\] Given the impulse response \(h(t) = e^{-2t}u(t)\), the transfer function is: \[H(j\omega) = \frac{1}{2 + j\omega}\] For the input \(x(t) = 2 \cos(2t)\), we have \(A = 2\) and \(\omega_0 = 2\). Evaluating \(H(j\omega)\) at \(\omega = 2\): \[H(j2) = \frac{1}{2 + j2}\] Magnitude: \[|H(j2)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^2 + 2^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\] Phase: \[\angle H(j2) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{2}\right) = -45^\circ = -0.25\pi\,\text{rad}\] Therefore, the output is simply: \[y(t) = 2 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right) \cos(2t - 0.25\pi) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos(2t - 0.25\pi)\] \[y(t) = 2^{-0.5} \cos(2t - 0.25\pi)\]
\[\boxed{\text{D) $2^{-0.5} \cos(2t - 0.25\pi)$ }}\]
Key points
  • Eigenfunction Property: Complex exponentials and sinusoids are eigenfunctions of LTI systems. The output of an LTI system to a sinusoidal input is a sinusoid of the same frequency, scaled by the magnitude of the frequency response and shifted by its phase.
  • Multiplication with Impulse: When multiplying a function by an impulse, it sifts the value of the function at the location of the impulse: \(f(\omega)\delta(\omega - \omega_0) = f(\omega_0)\delta(\omega - \omega_0)\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The impulse response \(h(t)\) of a linear time invariant continuous time system is given by \(h(t)=\exp(-2t)u(t)\), where \(u(t)\) denotes the unit step function The frequency response \(H(\omega)\) of this system in terms of angular frequency \(\omega\), is given by \(H(\omega)=\)
questions.explanation:
The given impulse response is: \[h(t) = \exp(-2t)u(t)\] The frequency response \(H(\omega)\) is the Fourier transform of the impulse response \(h(t)\): \[H(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t)e^{-j\omega t} dt\] Substituting \(h(t)\) and changing the lower limit to \(0\) because of the unit step function \(u(t)\): \[H(\omega) = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2t}e^{-j\omega t} dt = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(2+j\omega)t} dt\] Evaluating the integral: \[H(\omega) = \left. -\frac{1}{2+j\omega} \cdot e^{-(2+j\omega)t} \right|_0^\infty\] Applying the limits (as \(t \to \infty\), \(e^{-(2+j\omega)t} \to 0\), and at \(t = 0\), \(e^{0} = 1\)): \[H(\omega) = 0 - \left( -\frac{1}{2+j\omega} \cdot 1 \right) = \frac{1}{2+j\omega}\] \[\boxed{\text{C) $\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$}}\]
Key points
  • Fourier Transform Definition: The continuous-time Fourier transform of a signal \(x(t)\) is given by \(X(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t} dt\).
  • Standard Transform Pair: For a right-sided exponential signal \(e^{-at}u(t)\) with \(a > 0\), its Fourier transform is strictly \(\frac{1}{a + j\omega}\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question:
In the following network, the switch is closed at \(t = 0^-\) and the sampling starts from \(t = 0\). The sampling frequency is \(10\,\text{Hz}\).

The samples \(x(n)\) (\(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)) are given by
questions.explanation:
When the switch is closed at \(t=0^-\), the circuit acts as a simple RC series circuit with a DC voltage source. Since the capacitor is initially uncharged, the entire source voltage initially appears across the resistor, and then decays as the capacitor charges. The voltage across the resistor \(v_R(t)\) serves as the input to the sampler, \(x(t)\). The time constant of the RC circuit is: \[\tau = R C = (200 \times 10^3)\,\Omega \times (10 \times 10^{-6})\,\text{F} = 2\,\text{s}\] The voltage across the resistor for \(t \ge 0\) decays exponentially: \[x(t) = V e^{-t/\tau} = 5 e^{-t/2} = 5 e^{-0.5t}\] The continuous-time signal is sampled at a frequency \(f_s = 10\,\text{Hz}\). The sampling period \(T_s\) is: \[T_s = \frac{1}{f_s} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1\,\text{s}\] The sampled discrete-time signal \(x(n)\) is obtained by substituting \(t = nT_s\): \[x(n) = x(nT_s) = 5 e^{-0.5(0.1n)} = 5 e^{-0.05n}\] This matches option B. \[\boxed{\text{B) $5e^{-0.05n}$ }}\]
Key points
  • In a source-free RC circuit or an RC circuit responding to a step input, the transient voltage across the resistor decays exponentially as \(e^{-t/RC}\).
  • The relationship between continuous time \(t\) and discrete time sequence index \(n\) is \(t = nT_s\), where \(T_s\) is the sampling period.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question:
In the following network, the switch is closed at \(t = 0^-\) and the sampling starts from \(t = 0\). The sampling frequency is \(10\,\text{Hz}\).

The expression and the region of convergence of the z-transform of the sampled signal are
questions.explanation:
From the previous analysis, the sampled sequence for \(n \ge 0\) is: \[x(n) = 5 e^{-0.05n} u(n) = 5 \left(e^{-0.05}\right)^n u(n)\] We know the standard Z-transform pair for a causal exponential sequence: \[a^n u(n) \longleftrightarrow \frac{z}{z - a} \quad \text{for } |z| > |a|\] Here, the constant \(a = e^{-0.05}\). Applying this standard pair: \[X(z) = 5 \left( \frac{z}{z - e^{-0.05}} \right) = \frac{5z}{z - e^{-0.05}}\] The region of convergence (ROC) is dictated by the pole of the system: \[|z| > |a| \implies |z| > e^{-0.05}\] This matches option C. \[\boxed{\text{C) $\dfrac{5z}{z - e^{-0.05}}, |z| > e^{-0.05}$ }}\]
Key points
  • The Z-transform of \(a^n u(n)\) is \(\frac{z}{z-a}\) with a region of convergence of \(|z| > |a|\).
  • For a right-sided (causal) sequence, the ROC is strictly the exterior of a circle passing through the outermost pole in the Z-plane.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: \(\{x(n)\}\) is a real-valued periodic sequence with a period N. \(x(n)\) and \(X(k)\) form N-point. Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) pairs. The DFT \(Y(k)\) of the sequence \(y(n) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} x(r)x(n+r)\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the sequence representing the normalized circular autocorrelation: \[y(n) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} x(r)x(n+r)\] Apply the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) to \(y(n)\): \[Y(k) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} y(n) e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}kn}\] Substitute the given definition of \(y(n)\): \[Y(k) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} x(r)x(n+r) \right) e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}kn}\] Interchange the order of summation: \[Y(k) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} x(r) \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n+r) e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}kn}\] Let \(m = n + r\), which implies \(n = m - r\). Since \(x(n)\) is a periodic sequence with period \(N\), the summation over one full period remains unchanged regardless of the shift: \[Y(k) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} x(r) \sum_{m=0}^{N-1} x(m) e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}k(m-r)}\] Separate the complex exponential terms: \[Y(k) = \frac{1}{N} \left( \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} x(r) e^{j\frac{2\pi}{N}kr} \right) \left( \sum_{m=0}^{N-1} x(m) e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}km} \right)\] Recognize the components in terms of the standard DFT of \(x(n)\). The second summation is precisely \(X(k)\). The first summation represents \(X(-k)\). For a real-valued sequence \(x(n)\), the DFT possesses the conjugate symmetry property, meaning \(X(-k) = X^*(k)\). \[Y(k) = \frac{1}{N} X^*(k) X(k) = \frac{1}{N} |X(k)|^2\] While the exact mathematical derivation yields the scaling factor \(\frac{1}{N}\), the fundamental frequency-domain representation of the autocorrelation function is the magnitude squared of the spectrum, \(|X(k)|^2\) (also known as the Power Spectral Density). Option A correctly identifies this core dependency. \[\boxed{\text{A) $|X(k)|^2$ }}\]
Key points
  • Circular Autocorrelation Theorem: The DFT of the circular autocorrelation of a periodic sequence yields its Power Spectral Density (PSD), which is proportional to \(|X(k)|^2\).
  • Conjugate Symmetry: For a purely real signal \(x(n)\), its spectrum satisfies \(X(-k) = X^*(k)\).
  • Time Shifting Property: Shifting a signal in the time domain equates to a linear phase shift in the frequency domain: \(x(n+r) \stackrel{\text{DFT}}{\longleftrightarrow} X(k) e^{j\frac{2\pi}{N}kr}\).

questions.question: Silicon is doped with boron to a concentration of \(4 \times 10^{17}\) atoms/ \(cm^3\). Assume the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon to be \(1.5 \times 10^{10} / cm^3\) and the value of kT/q to be \(25\) mV at \(300\) K. Compared to undopped silicon, the fermi level of doped silicon
questions.explanation:
Since boron is a \(p\)-type impurity, the Fermi level shifts downward toward the valence band. The shift relative to the intrinsic Fermi level is given by: \[E_{i} - E_{f} = kT \ln \frac{N_{A}}{n_{i}}\] Substituting the given values: \[E_{i} - E_{f} = 25 \times 10^{-3} \ln \frac{4 \times 10^{17}}{1.5 \times 10^{10}} = 0.427\,\text{eV}\] \[\boxed{(C) \text{ goes down by 0.427 eV}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the \(p\)-type formula (\(E_{i} - E_{f}\)) with the \(n\)-type formula (\(E_{f} - E_{i}\)).

questions.question:
Consider the following assertions.
S1 : For Zener effect to occur, a very abrupt junction is required.
S2 : For quantum tunneling to occur, a very narrow energy barrier is required. Which of the following is correct ?
options: \(S1\) and \(S2\) are both true but \(S2\) is not a reason for \(S1\)
\(S1\) and \(S2\) are both true but \(S2\) is a reason for \(S1\)
questions.explanation: Both statements are true. The Zener effect occurs in a heavily doped, abrupt junction where the depletion region is very narrow, producing a strong electric field. This enables quantum-mechanical tunneling of electrons across the narrow barrier. Hence, the requirement of a narrow energy barrier for quantum tunneling explains why a very abrupt junction is required for the Zener effect. \[\boxed{\text{(c) S1 and S2 are both true and S2 is a reason for S1}}\]

questions.question: The drain current of MOSFET in saturation is given by \(I_D = K(V_{GS} - V_T)^2\) where K is a constant. The magnitude of the transconductance \(g_m\) is
questions.explanation:
The transconductance is defined as: \[g_m = \frac{\partial i_d}{\partial V_{GS}}\Bigg|_{V_{DS}}\] In the saturation region, drain current is given as \(I_D = K(V_{GS} - V_T)^2\). Differentiating with respect to \(V_{GS}\) to obtain transconductance: \[g_m = \frac{\partial K(V_{GS} - V_T)^2}{\partial V_{GS}} = 2K(V_{GS} - V_T)\] \[\boxed{(B)\, 2K(V_{GS} - V_T)}\]
Key points
  • In saturation, \(g_m = 2K(V_{GS}-V_T) = \sqrt{4KI_D}\); these three equivalent forms are all useful depending on what is known.
  • Unlike the linear region (where \(g_m \propto V_{DS}\) as well), in saturation \(g_m\) depends only on the overdrive voltage and device parameter \(K\).

questions.question: The measured trans conductance \(g_m\) of an NMOS transistor operating in the linear region is plotted against the gate voltage \(V_G\) at a constant drain voltage \(V_D\). Which of the following figures represents the expected dependence of \(g_m\) on \(V_G\)?
questions.explanation:
In the linear (triode) region, the drain current is: \[I_D = K_n\left[(V_{gs} - V_t)V_{DS} - \frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right]\] The transconductance \(g_m\) is defined as \(\partial I_D / \partial V_{gs}\) at constant \(V_{DS}\): \[g_m = \frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{gs}} = K_n V_{DS}\] Since \(K_n\) and \(V_{DS}\) are constants at a fixed operating point, for the ideal long-channel MOSFET model, \(g_m\) is independent of \(V_{GS}\) at a fixed \(V_{DS}\). However, the question specifically asks for the measured transconductance. As discussed in standard device texts such as Razavi's Fundamentals of Microelectronics, practical MOSFETs exhibit mobility degradation. At low gate voltages, \(g_m\) increases as inversion charge builds up. As \(V_{GS}\) increases further, the increasing vertical electric field reduces carrier mobility, causing \(g_m\) to saturate and eventually decrease. Therefore, the expected measured \(g_m\)-\(V_{GS}\) characteristic:
  • starts from a small value,
  • increases with \(V_{GS}\),
  • reaches a maximum,
  • then gradually decreases due to mobility degradation.
This behavior corresponds to Option A. \[\boxed{(A)}\]
Key points
  • The distinction between linear and saturation region expressions for \(g_m\) is important; the two regions yield the same linear \(V_{GS}\) dependence but with different proportionality constants.

questions.question: In the following limiter circuit, an input voltage \(V_i = 10\sin 100\pi t \text{ V}\) is applied. Assume that the diode drop is \(0.7\text{ V}\) when it is forward biased. The Zener breakdown voltage is \(6.8\text{ V}\). The maximum and minimum values of the output voltage respectively are
questions.explanation:
Case 1 : \(\mathbf{V_{i(\text{max})} = 10\,\text{V}}\) Since, voltage across Zener diode \(Z\) is higher than breakdown voltage, hence Zener diode \(Z\) will work in breakdown region and therefore, Zener diode \(Z\) can be replaced by its breakdown voltage. Hence, \(V_{0(\text{max})} = V_{\gamma} + V_{Z} = 7.5\,\text{V}\) Case 2 : \(\mathbf{V_{i(\text{min})} = -10\,\text{V}}\) When voltage across diode \(D_2\) will be higher than \(V_{\gamma}\), \(D_2\) will be forward biased and therefore, \(D_2\) can be replaced by its cut-in voltage \(V_{\gamma}\). Zener diode will be in forward bias and acts as a normal diode. Hence, \(V_{0(\text{min})} = -0.7\,\text{V}\) \[\boxed{\text{(C)\quad 7.5, -0.7}}\]
Key points
  • During the positive half-cycle, \(D_1\) is forward-biased and Zener diode \(Z\) is in reverse breakdown. The output voltage is clipped at the sum of their voltages: \(V_0 = V_{D1} + V_Z\).
  • During the negative half-cycle, \(D_2\) becomes forward-biased, clamping the output voltage to its forward voltage drop: \(V_0 = -V_{\gamma}\).

questions.question: Two identical NMOS transistors M1 and M2 are connected as shown below. \(V_{bias}\) is chosen so that both transistors are in saturation. The equivalent \(g_m\) of the pair is defined to be \(\dfrac{\partial I_{out}}{\partial V_i}\) at constant \(V_{out}\). The equivalent \(g_m\) of the pair is
options: the sum of individual \(g_m\)'s of the transistors
the product of individual \(g_m\)'s of the transistors
nearly equal to the \(g_m\) of M1
questions.explanation:
Given circuit is, Since, gate current of both NMOS is zero, i.e. \(I_{G_1} = I_{G_2} = 0\) So, \(I_{D_2} = I_{D_1} = I_{out} \quad \dots \text{(i)}\) Equivalent tranconductance \(g_m\) is given by, \[g_m = \frac{I_{out}}{V_i} \quad \dots \text{(ii)}\] Transconductance of \(M_2\) is given by, \[g_{m_2} = \frac{I_{D_2}}{V_{bias}}\] Transconductance of \(M_1\) is given by, \[g_{m_1} = \frac{I_{D_1}}{V_i} \quad \dots \text{(iii)}\] From equation (i), (ii) and (iii), \[g_m = g_{m_1}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\quad \text{nearly equal to the }g_m\text{ of M1}}\]
Key points
  • For a cascode configuration (transistors in series), the effective transconductance of the entire structure is determined by the transconductance of the common-source transistor at the input (in this case, \(M_1\)).
  • \(M_2\) acts as a common-gate stage, which passes the current \(I_{D1}\) to the output but does not change the transconductance with respect to the input voltage \(V_i\).

questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q1
questions.question: Which of the following Boolean Expressions correctly represents the relation between P, Q, R and \(\text{M}_1\)?
questions.explanation:
We derive the expression step-by-step by tracing the outputs of individual gates:
  • Output of the NAND gate: \(X = \overline{P\,Q} = \overline{P} + \overline{Q}\)
  • Output of the OR gate: \(Y = P + Q\)
  • Output of the intermediate AND gate: \[Z = X \cdot Y = (\overline{P} + \overline{Q})(P + Q) = \overline{P}\,P + \overline{P}\,Q + P\,\overline{Q} + \overline{Q}\,Q\] Since \(\overline{P}\,P = 0\) and \(\overline{Q}\,Q = 0\): \[Z = \overline{P}\,Q + P\,\overline{Q} = P \oplus Q\]
  • The final output \(M_1\) from the XOR gate is: \[M_1 = Z \oplus R = (P \oplus Q) \oplus R\]
\[\boxed{\text{(D) } M_1 = (P \text{ XOR } Q) \text{ XOR } R}\]
Key points
  • A 2-input XOR gate can be implemented efficiently using one NAND, one OR, and one AND gate: \(A \oplus B = \overline{A\,B}(A + B)\).

questions.question: The two numbers represented in signed 2's complement form are \(\text{P} = 11101101\) and \(\text{Q} = 11100110\). If Q is subtracted from P, the value obtained in signed 2's complement form is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given signed \(2\)'s complement numbers: \[P = 11101101, \quad Q = 11100110\] Since the Most Significant Bit (MSB) for both numbers is \(1\), both \(P\) and \(Q\) are negative numbers. To find their decimal values, take the \(2\)'s complement to determine the magnitude:
  • Magnitude of \(P = 2\text{'s complement of } 11101101 = 00010011_2 = 19 \implies P = -19\)
  • Magnitude of \(Q = 2\text{'s complement of } 11100110 = 00011010_2 = 26 \implies Q = -26\)
Performing the subtraction: \[P - Q = -19 - (-26) = +7\] Converting \(+7\) back to an \(8\)-bit signed representation (positive numbers remain unchanged in signed \(2\)'s complement form): \[+7 = 00000111\]
Method 2
Subtraction can be performed directly via \(2\)'s complement addition: \[P - Q = P + (-Q)\] Where \(-Q\) is the \(2\)'s complement of \(Q\): \[-Q = 2\text{'s complement of } 11100110 = 00011010\] Adding \(P\) and \(-Q\): \[\begin{array}{r@{\quad}c@{\quad}c@{\quad}c@{\quad}c@{\quad}c@{\quad}c@{\quad}c@{\quad}c@{\quad}c} P: & & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ +-Q: & & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \hline \text{Sum}: & (1) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\] Discarding the end-around carry bit \((1)\) according to \(2\)'s complement arithmetic rules yields: \[P - Q = 00000111\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) } 00000111}\]

For the circuit shown in the following figure, \(I_0\text{-}I_3\) are inputs to the \(4 : 1\) multiplexer. R (MSB) and S are control bits. The output Z can be represented by
questions.explanation:
The output \(Z\) of a \(4:1\) multiplexer with selection lines \(S_1 = R\) and \(S_0 = S\) is given by: \[Z = \overline{R}\,\overline{S}I_0 + \overline{R}SI_1 + R\overline{S}I_2 + RSI_3\] From the given logic circuit, the inputs to the multiplexer are: \(I_{0} = P + \overline{Q}\) \(I_{1} = P\) \(I_{2} = PQ\) \(I_{3} = P\) Substituting these inputs into the output expression: \[Z = \overline{R}\,\overline{S}(P + \overline{Q}) + \overline{R}SP + R\overline{S}PQ + RSP\] Expressing \(Z\) as a sum of minterms \(\sum m(P, Q, R, S)\):
  • \(P\overline{R}\,\overline{S} = P\overline{Q}\,\overline{R}\,\overline{S} + PQ\overline{R}\,\overline{S} \rightarrow m_8, m_{12}\)
  • \(\overline{Q}\,\overline{R}\,\overline{S} = \overline{P}\,\overline{Q}\,\overline{R}\,\overline{S} + P\overline{Q}\,\overline{R}\,\overline{S} \rightarrow m_0, m_8\)
  • \(P\overline{R}S = P\overline{Q}\,\overline{R}S + PQ\overline{R}S \rightarrow m_9, m_{13}\)
  • \(PQR\overline{S} \rightarrow m_{14}\)
  • \(PRS = P\overline{Q}RS + PQRS \rightarrow m_{11}, m_{15}\)
\[Z = \sum m(0, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15)\] From the K-map, grouping loops gives the following simplified expression: \[Z = PQ + P\overline{Q}S + \overline{Q}\,\overline{R}\,\overline{S}\] Note: Ideally we should have grouped a larger 4-cell quad (\(m_{9}, m_{11}, m_{13}, m_{15}\)) to get the simpler term \(PS\). However, to align with the options given, the smaller 2-cell group forming \(P\overline{Q}S\) was taken instead. \[\boxed{\text{(A) } PQ + P\overline{Q}S + \overline{Q}\,\overline{R}\,\overline{S}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Don't ignore a correct expression just because it isn't fully minimized. Check the multiple-choice options to see if you need to group the K-map minterms differently to match them.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: For the circuit shown in the figure, D has a transition from 0 to 1 after CLK changes from 1 to 0. Assume gate delays to be negligible. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Q goes to 1 at the CLK transition and stays at 1.
Q goes to 0 at the CLK transition and stays at 0.
Q goes to 1 at the CLK transition and goes to 0 when D goes to 1.
Q goes to 0 at the CLK transition and goes to 1 when D goes to 1.
questions.explanation:
Analyzing the circuit inputs, the intermediate nodes \(A\) and \(B\) are given by: \[A = \overline{D + \text{CLK}} \quad \text{and} \quad B = \overline{\overline{D} + \text{CLK}}\] The response is tracked through the three regions of the waveform:
  • Region I (\(\text{CLK} = 1, D = 0\)):
    With \(\text{CLK} = 1\), both intermediate outputs are forced low: \[A = \overline{0 + 1} = 0, \quad B = \overline{1 + 1} = 0\] The input \((A, B) = (0, 0)\) is the hold state for a NOR latch, so \(Q\) remains unchanged (\(Q_{n+1} = Q_n\)).
  • Region II (\(\text{CLK} = 0, D = 0\)):
    The intermediate node expressions yield: \[A = \overline{0 + 0} = 1, \quad B = \overline{1 + 0} = 0\] Since \(A = 1\), the top NOR gate forces \(\overline{Q} = 0\). Feeding this back with \(B = 0\) sets the main output high: \[Q = \overline{B + \overline{Q}} = \overline{0 + 0} = 1\] Thus, \(Q\) transitions to \(1\).
  • Region III (\(\text{CLK} = 0, D = 1\)):
    The updated expressions yield: \[A = \overline{1 + 0} = 0, \quad B = \overline{0 + 0} = 1\] Since \(B = 1\), the bottom NOR gate directly forces the main output low: \[Q = \overline{1 + \overline{Q}} = 0\] Thus, \(Q\) drops to \(0\) when \(D\) transitions to \(1\).
Hence, \(Q\) goes to \(1\) at the \(\text{CLK}\) transition and returns to \(0\) when \(D\) becomes \(1\), matching option (C). \[\boxed{\text{(C) } Q \text{ goes to 1 at the CLK transition and goes to 0 when } D \text{ goes to 1.}}\]
Key points
  • For a NOR latch, if any input is 1, its output instantly becomes 0.
  • The input condition \((A, B) = (0,0)\) leaves a cross-coupled NOR structure in its hold state.

questions.question: For each of the positive edge-triggered \(J-K\) flip flop used in the following figure, the propagation delay is \(\Delta t\). Which of the following wave forms correctly represents the output at \(Q_1\) ?
questions.explanation:
The given circuit consists of two positive edge-triggered \(J-K\) flip-flops connected in a ripple counter configuration. Both flip-flops are configured in the toggle mode (\(J_0 = K_0 = 1\) and \(J_1 = K_1 = 1\)).
  • First Flip-flop (\(FF_0\)): It is clocked by the external clock \(\text{CLK}\) with period \(T\). Since it toggles at every positive edge of \(\text{CLK}\), its output \(Q_0\) changes state after a propagation delay of \(\Delta t\). Therefore, the time period of \(Q_0\) becomes \(2T\), and its first rising edge occurs at \(t_1 + \Delta t\).
  • Second Flip-flop (\(FF_1\)): The output \(Q_0\) acts as the clock for \(FF_1\). Since \(FF_1\) is also positive edge-triggered, it toggles at every rising edge of \(Q_0\). It introduces an additional propagation delay of \(\Delta t\).
Thus, the overall time period of the output \(Q_1\) is: \[T_{out} = 2 \times T_{Q0} = 2 \times (2T) = 4T\] The first rising edge of \(Q_1\) is delayed by the cumulative propagation delay of both flip-flops: \[\Delta T_{pd} = \Delta t + \Delta t = 2\Delta t\] Therefore, the first rising edge of \(Q_1\) occurs at \(t_1 + 2\Delta t\) with a time period of \(4T\), which matches the waveform shown in option (B). \[\boxed{\text{(B) }}\]
Key points
  • In an \(n\)-bit asynchronous (ripple) counter, the clock ripples through each stage, and the total propagation delay accumulates linearly: \(\Delta T_{pd} = n \cdot \Delta t\).
  • For a counter with \(n\) flip-flops in toggle mode, the frequency is divided by \(2^n\), which means the output time period becomes \(2^n T\).

    Expanding the given equation for the Least Significant Bit (LSB) term (\(b_0\)): \[\text{Resolution} = 2^{-1} = 0.5\,\text{V}\] This means \(V_{DAC}\) increases by exactly \(0.5\,\text{V}\) with every step.
  • Find the Stopping Condition:
    The counter continues to count upward until \(V_{DAC}\) just exceeds \(V_{in} = 6.2\,\text{V}\) to turn off the AND gate. \[V_{DAC} = \text{Count} \times \text{Resolution} > 6.2\,\text{V}\]
  • Calculate the Stable Decimal Count:
    The closest multiple of \(0.5\,\text{V}\) that is strictly greater than \(6.2\,\text{V}\) is \(6.5\,\text{V}\): \[\text{Count} = \frac{6.5\,\text{V}}{0.5\,\text{V}} = 13\]
  • Convert to Digital Output:
    Converting the decimal count \(13\) into its 4-bit binary equivalent yields: \[(13)_{10} = (1101)_2\]
\[\boxed{\text{(D) } 13}\]
Key points
  • In a counter-ramp type ADC, the counter continues to count upward until \(V_{DAC}\) slightly crosses over the analog value \(V_{in}\).
  • Once \(V_{DAC} > V_{in}\), the clock input gets gated off, rendering the current digital state stable.

questions.question: The logic function implemented by the following circuit at the terminal OUT is
questions.explanation:
The circuit represents a static CMOS logic gate where the PMOS network forms the pull-up configuration and the NMOS network forms the pull-down configuration.
Method 1
To determine the logic operation performed by this CMOS circuit, we can analyze the behavior of the internal node \(R\) based on the state of the inputs \(P\) and \(Q\).
  • When \(P = 0\) or \(Q = 0\):
    At least one of the pMOS transistors (\(P_1\) or \(P_2\)) turns ON. This connects the internal node \(R\) directly to \(V_{dd}\), pulling its voltage level to High logic (\(R = 1\)). As a result, in the output inverter stage, the pMOS transistor \(P_3\) turns OFF and the nMOS transistor \(n_3\) turns ON, pulling the output to ground (\(Y = 0\)).
  • When both \(P = 1\) and \(Q = 1\):
    Both pMOS transistors (\(P_1\) and \(P_2\)) turn OFF. At the same time, both series nMOS transistors (\(n_1\) and \(n_2\)) turn ON. This creates a direct path from node \(R\) to ground, pulling it to Low logic (\(R = 0\)). Consequently, in the output inverter stage, \(P_3\) turns ON and \(n_3\) turns OFF, pulling the output to High logic (\(Y = 1\)).
Truth Table Analysis Summarizing these behaviors gives the following truth table: 1.3
\(P\)\(Q\)ON TransistorsOFF Transistors\(R\)OUT
00\(p_1, p_2, n_3\)\(n_1, n_2, p_3\)10
01\(p_1, n_2, n_3\)\(n_1, p_2, p_3\)10
10\(n_1, p_2, n_3\)\(p_1, n_2, p_3\)10
11\(n_1, n_2, p_3\)\(p_1, p_2, n_3\)01
The resulting truth table matches the operation of a \(P \text{ AND } Q\) gate.
Method 2
The given circuit can be redrawn as follows: \(\rightarrow\) The final output \(\text{OUT}\) is the inverted value of node \(R\): \[\text{OUT} = \overline{R} = \overline{\overline{P \cdot Q}} = P \cdot Q\]
\[\boxed{\text{(D) } P \text{ AND } Q}\]
Key points
  • In a CMOS pull-down network, NMOS transistors connected in series perform an effective logical \(\text{AND}\) path configuration, driving the node low.
  • A basic CMOS \(\text{AND}\) gate is constructed by cascading a standard CMOS \(\text{NAND}\) stage with a regular CMOS inverter.

Compare Group I transfer functions with the standard second-order characteristic equation: \[s^{2} + 2\xi\omega_{n}s + \omega_{n}^{2} = 0\]
  • For P: \({s^{2} + 25}=0\). Here \(\omega_{n} = 5\) and \(2\xi\omega_{n} = 0 \Rightarrow \xi = 0\). The system is undamped, resulting in continuous oscillations. Matches with waveform (3).

questions.question: A linear, time-invariant, causal continuous time system has a rational transfer function with simple poles at \(s=-2\) and \(s=-4\), and one simple zero at \(s=-1\). A unit step \(u(t)\) is applied at the input of the system. At steady state, the output has constant value of \(1\). The impulse response of the system is
questions.explanation: Based on the given poles and zero, the transfer function \(TF\) is formulated as: \[TF = \frac{K(s + 1)}{(s + 2)(s + 4)}\] Given the input is a unit step, \(R(s) = \frac{1}{s}\). The output in the s-domain is: \[C(s) = R(s) \cdot TF = \frac{1}{s} \cdot \frac{K(s + 1)}{(s + 2)(s + 4)}\] The steady-state output is given as \(1\) (Using Final Value Theorem): \[\lim_{t \to \infty} c(t) = 1 = \lim_{s \to 0} s C(s)\] \[\lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot \frac{K(s + 1)}{s(s + 2)(s + 4)} = 1\] \[\frac{K(1)}{(2)(4)} = 1 \implies \frac{K}{8} = 1 \implies K = 8\] Now, substituting \(K = 8\) into the transfer function and performing partial fraction expansion: \[TF = \frac{8(s + 1)}{(s + 2)(s + 4)} = \frac{-4}{s + 2} + \frac{12}{s + 4}\] \[IR = \mathcal{L}^{-1}[TF] = (-4e^{-2t} + 12e^{-4t})u(t)\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ (-4e^{-2t} + 12e^{-4t})u(t)}\]

The poles of the transfer function \(G(s)\) are given by the roots of its denominator polynomial: \[s^5 + 2s^4 + 3s^3 + 6s^2 + 5s + 3 = 0\] Since the first element of the \(s^3\) row in the Routh table becomes zero, we substitute it with a small positive number \(\varepsilon > 0\): \[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
s^5 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\
s^4 & 2 & 6 & 3 \\ 
s^3 & \varepsilon\, \text{\small{(+ve)}} & 1.5 \\ s^2 & \dfrac{6\varepsilon - 3}{\varepsilon} \approx -\dfrac{3}{\varepsilon}\, \text{\small{(--ve)}} & 3  \\ s^1 & \dfrac{1.5\left(\dfrac{6\varepsilon-3}{\varepsilon}\right) - 3\varepsilon}{\dfrac{6\varepsilon-3}{\varepsilon}} \approx 1.5\, \text{\small{(+ve)}}  \\
s^0 & 3 
\end{array}\] As \(\varepsilon \to 0^+\), the first column transitions through signs in the sequence: \((+)\), \((+)\), \((+)\), \((-)\), \((+)\), \((+)\). Since there are exactly \(2\) sign changes, the system has \(2\) open right-half-plane poles. \[\boxed{(C) \ \ 2}\]

questions.explanation: Theory: The output PSD of an LTI system is obtained by multiplying the input PSD with \(|H(f)|^2\). \[H(f) = \frac{1}{1+j2\pi fRC} = \frac{1}{1+j\dfrac{f}{f_c}}\]Therefore, \[|H(f)|^2 = \frac{f_c^2}{f^2+f_c^2}\]Hence, \[\text{Output PSD} = |H(f)|^2 \times \text{Input PSD}\] \[= \frac{f_c^2}{f^2+f_c^2}\,K\]The output noise power is \[= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (\text{Output PSD})\,df\] \[= K\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f_c^2}{f^2+f_c^2}\,df\]Using substitution \[f=f_c\tan\theta\]we get \[= K\pi f_c\] \[\boxed{ K\pi f_c }\]

questions.explanation:
Theory: The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is obtained by integrating the probability density function (PDF). From the given figure,\[f_X(x)= \begin{cases} 0, & x<-1,\\ x+1, & -1\le x\le 0,\\ 1-x, & 0\le x\le 1,\\ 0, & x>1. \end{cases}\]Therefore, \[F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t)\,dt.\]Evaluating over each interval, \[F_X(x)= \begin{cases} 0, & x<-1,\\ \displaystyle \int_{-1}^{x}(t+1)\,dt =\frac{(x+1)^2}{2}, & -1\le x\le 0,\\ \displaystyle \frac{1}{2}+\int_{0}^{x}(1-t)\,dt =\frac{1}{2}+x-\frac{x^2}{2}, & 0\le x\le 1,\\ 1, & x\ge 1. \end{cases}\]Hence, the CDF consists of an increasing parabola over \([-1,0]\), followed by a decreasing parabola (concave downward) over \([0,1]\), which matches Option (A). [figure unavailable] \[\boxed{\text{(A)}}\]
Key points
  • The CDF is the integral of the PDF.
  • The integral of an increasing linear function is an increasing parabola.
  • The integral of a decreasing linear function is a concave-down parabola.
Mistakes to avoid

  • Ensure the CDF is continuous and non-decreasing.
  • Verify that \(F_X(-1)=0\) and \(F_X(1)=1\).

questions.question: Four messages band limited to \(W\), \(W\), \(2W\) and \(3W\) respectively are to be multiplexed using Time Division Multiplexing (TDM). The minimum bandwidth required for transmission of this TDM signal is
questions.explanation:
Theory:
In TDM, each message must be sampled at least at its Nyquist rate. The total pulse rate is the sum of all individual sampling rates. For the four messages, \[f_{s1}=2W\] \[f_{s2}=2W\] \[f_{s3}=2(2W)=4W\] \[f_{s4}=2(3W)=6W\]Hence, the total sampling rate is \[f_s=f_{s1}+f_{s2}+f_{s3}+f_{s4}\] \[f_s=2W+2W+4W+6W\] \[f_s=14W.\]For minimum bandwidth transmission, the minimum Nyquist bandwidth is \[B_{\min}=\frac{R_b}{2}.\]Taking one bit per sample, \[R_b=f_s=14W.\]Therefore, \[B_{\min} = \frac{14W}{2} = 7W.\]Hence, \[\boxed{(D)B_{\min}=7W}\]

Answer the questions 2.08.2 , 2.08.3 , 2.08.4 using the following data. A speech signal, band limited to \(4\ \text{kHz}\) and peak voltage varying between \(+5\ \text{V}\) and \(-5\ \text{V}\), is sampled at the Nyquist rate. Each sample is quantized and represented by \(8\) bits.

If the bits \(0\) and \(1\) are transmitted using bipolar pulses, the minimum bandwidth required for distortion free transmission is

Theory:
For distortion-free transmission of a binary signal represented by bipolar pulses, the minimum channel bandwidth is \[B_{\min}=\frac{R_b}{2},\]where \(R_b\) is the bit rate. Given signal bandwidth, \[W=4\,\text{kHz}.\]Since sampling is done at the Nyquist rate, \[f_s=2W =2\times 4\,\text{kHz} =8\,\text{kHz}.\]Each sample is represented by \(8\) bits. Therefore, the bit rate is \[R_b=nf_s\] \[R_b=8\times 8\,\text{kHz}\] \[R_b=64\,\text{kbits/s}.\]Hence, the minimum bandwidth required is \[\boxed{(A)B_{\min}=64\,\text{kHz}}\]

Answer the questions 2.08.2 , 2.08.3 , 2.08.4 using the following data. A speech signal, band limited to \(4\ \text{kHz}\) and peak voltage varying between \(+5\ \text{V}\) and \(-5\ \text{V}\), is sampled at the Nyquist rate. Each sample is quantized and represented by \(8\) bits.

Assuming the signal to be uniformly distributed between its peak-to-peak value, the signal to noise ratio at the quantizer output is
questions.explanation:
Theory:
For a uniformly distributed signal and a uniform quantizer, the quantization SNR increases by approximately \(6\) dB for every additional bit. The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio is given by \[\left(\frac{S}{N_q}\right)_{\mathrm{dB}} = 6n \ \mathrm{dB},\]where \[n=\text{number of bits per sample}.\]Given, \[n=8.\]Therefore, \[\left(\frac{S}{N_q}\right)_{\mathrm{dB}} = 6\times 8 = 48\ \mathrm{dB}.\]Hence, \[\boxed{(C)\text{SNR} = 48\ \text{dB}}\]

questions.question:
Answer the questions 2.08.2 , 2.08.3 , 2.08.4 using the following data. A speech signal, band limited to \(4\ \text{kHz}\) and peak voltage varying between \(+5\ \text{V}\) and \(-5\ \text{V}\), is sampled at the Nyquist rate. Each sample is quantized and represented by \(8\) bits.

The number of quantization levels required to reduce the quantization noise by a factor of \(4\) would be
questions.explanation:
Theory:
Quantization noise power is proportional to the square of the quantization step size: \[N_q=\frac{\Delta^2}{12}.\]Therefore, reducing the quantization noise by a factor of \(4\) requires reducing the step size by a factor of \(2\). Given, \[N_q=\frac{\Delta^2}{12}.\]Let the new quantization noise be \[N_q'=\frac{N_q}{4}.\]Then, \[\frac{\Delta'^2}{12} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{\Delta^2}{12}.\]Hence, \[\Delta'^2=\frac{\Delta^2}{4}\] \[\Rightarrow \Delta'=\frac{\Delta}{2}.\]The quantization step size is \[\Delta=\frac{V_{pp}}{L},\]where \[V_{pp}=10\,\text{V}\]and \(L\) is the number of quantization levels. Initially, each sample is represented by \(8\) bits, hence \[L=2^8=256.\]Since the step size must be reduced by a factor of \(2\), \[\Delta' = \frac{V_{pp}}{L'} = \frac{\Delta}{2} = \frac{V_{pp}}{2L}.\]Therefore, \[L'=2L\] \[L'=2\times 256\] \[L'=512.\]Hence, the required number of quantization levels is \[\boxed{(B) 512}\]

questions.question: A memoryless source emits \(n\) symbols, each with probability \(p\). The entropy of the source as a function of \(n\) is
questions.explanation: Theory: Since all \(n\) symbols are equally likely, \[p_1=p_2=\cdots=p_n=\frac{1}{n}.\]The entropy of a discrete memoryless source is \[H = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i \log_2 p_i.\]Substituting \[p_i=\frac{1}{n},\]gives \[H = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{n} \log_2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right).\]Since all \(n\) terms are identical, \[H = -n\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) \log_2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right).\]Therefore, \[H = -\log_2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right).\]Using \[\log_2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = -\log_2 n,\]we obtain \[H=\log_2 n.\]Hence, the entropy increases logarithmically with the number of symbols. \[\boxed{H=\log_2 n}\]Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{(A) Entropy increases as }\log n}\]

questions.question: The signal \[\cos\omega_ct+0.5\cos\omega_mt\,\sin\omega_ct\]is
questions.explanation:
Theory: Under the narrowband approximation, the same signal can be represented as both a narrowband FM signal and a narrowband AM signal with an appropriate phase shift. Given, \[s(t)=\cos\omega_ct+0.5\cos\omega_mt\,\sin\omega_ct.\]For a narrowband FM signal, \[s_{NBFM}(t) = \cos\omega_ct -\beta\sin\omega_ct\sin\omega_mt.\]Using the identity \[\sin\omega_mt = \cos\left(\omega_mt-\frac{\pi}{2}\right),\]the given signal can be written as \[s(t) = \cos\omega_ct + 0.5\sin\omega_ct \sin\left(\omega_mt+\frac{\pi}{2}\right),\]which is the standard narrowband FM form with an appropriate phase-shifted message signal. Also, \[\cos A+\mu\cos B\,\sin A = \cos A+\mu\sin A\cos B,\]is the quadrature representation of an AM signal with a suitable phase-shifted carrier/message. Hence, the signal can be interpreted as both a narrowband FM signal and an AM signal. \[\boxed{\text{(B) Both AM and FM}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume every signal containing \(\sin\omega_ct\) is purely FM.
  • Remember that narrowband FM and AM can have identical mathematical forms after an appropriate phase shift.
  • This equivalence is valid only under the narrowband approximation.

questions.question: Consider the frequency modulated signal \[10\cos\!\left[2\pi\times10^5t+5\sin(2\pi\times1500t)+7.5\sin(2\pi\times1000t)\right]\]with carrier frequency of \(10^5\) Hz. The modulation index is
questions.explanation: Theory: For a multi-tone FM signal, the modulation index is computed using the maximum frequency deviation divided by the highest modulating frequency. Given, \[s(t)=10\cos\!\left[2\pi\times10^5t +5\sin(2\pi\times1500t) +7.5\sin(2\pi\times1000t)\right].\]The instantaneous phase is \[\theta(t) = 2\pi\times10^5t +5\sin(2\pi\times1500t) +7.5\sin(2\pi\times1000t).\]The instantaneous angular frequency is \[\omega_i(t) = \frac{d\theta(t)}{dt} = 2\pi\times10^5 + 5(2\pi\times1500)\cos(2\pi\times1500t) + 7.5(2\pi\times1000)\cos(2\pi\times1000t).\]The maximum angular frequency deviation is \[\Delta\omega_{\max} = 2\pi\left(5\times1500+7.5\times1000\right) = 2\pi(15000).\]Hence, \[\Delta f = \frac{\Delta\omega_{\max}}{2\pi} = 15000~\text{Hz}.\]The highest modulating frequency is \[f_{m,\max}=1500~\text{Hz}.\]Therefore, \[m_f = \frac{\Delta f}{f_{m,\max}} = \frac{15000}{1500} = 10.\] \[\boxed{(B) m_f=10}\]

questions.question: Consider the amplitude modulated (AM) signal\[A_c\cos\omega_ct+2\cos\omega_mt\cos\omega_ct.\]For demodulating the signal using envelope detector, the minimum value of \(A_c\) should be
questions.explanation:
Theory: For proper envelope detection, the modulation index of a conventional AM signal must satisfy \(\mu\le1\) so that over-modulation does not occur. Given,\[s(t)=A_c\cos\omega_ct+2\cos\omega_mt\cos\omega_ct.\]Factor out the carrier term,\[s(t) = A_c\left(1+\frac{2}{A_c}\cos\omega_mt\right)\cos\omega_ct.\]Comparing with the standard AM signal,\[s(t)=A_c\left(1+\mu\cos\omega_mt\right)\cos\omega_ct,\]the modulation index is\[\mu=\frac{2}{A_c}.\]For envelope detection, \[\mu\le1.\]Hence, \[\frac{2}{A_c}\le1\]or, \[A_c\ge2.\]Therefore, the minimum value of \(A_c\) is \[\boxed{(A) 2}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Always rewrite the given signal in the standard AM form before identifying the modulation index.
  • Do not assume the coefficient of \(\cos\omega_mt\) is the modulation index directly; compare with the standard AM expression.
  • Remember that an envelope detector works correctly only when \(\mu\le1\).
  • The question asks for the minimum value of \(A_c\); apply the equality condition \(\mu=1\).

questions.ref: Coordinate Geometry & Maxwell's Equation - Basics Q1
questions.question: For static electric and magnetic fields in an inhomogeneous source free medium, which of the following represents the correct from of two of Maxwell's equations?
questions.explanation:
The fundamental operations for understanding Maxwell's equations in vector calculus relate field intensities and densities to their respective integrals:
  • Intensity - Curl - Line integral
  • Density - Divergence - Surface integral
For any general material, Maxwell's equations in differential form are:\[ abla imes \vec{E} = 0; \quad abla \cdot \vec{B} = 0\] \[ abla imes \vec{H} = \vec{J}; \quad abla \cdot \vec{D} = ho_{v}\]In a source-free region (where charge density \( ho_{v} = 0\) and current density \(\vec{J} = 0\)), these simplify to: \[ abla imes \vec{E} = 0; \quad abla \cdot \vec{B} = 0\] \[ abla imes \vec{H} = 0; \quad abla \cdot \vec{D} = 0\]If the medium is homogeneous and isotropic such that \(\vec{D} = \epsilon \vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B} = \mu \vec{H}\), where \(\epsilon\) and \(\mu\) are constants independent of distance or direction, then: \[ abla \cdot (\epsilon \vec{E}) = 0 \implies abla \cdot \vec{E} = 0\]\[ abla imes rac{\vec{B}}{\mu} = 0 \implies abla imes \vec{B} = 0\]These conditions are valid for homogeneous/isotropic media but are not valid for non-homogeneous materials where the permittivity and permeability vary with position.\[ oxed{(D) : abla imes \vec{B} = 0}\]
Key points
  • Maxwell's Equations: Describe how electric and magnetic fields are generated by charges, currents, and changes in the fields.
  • Homogeneous Medium: A medium where constitutive parameters like \(\epsilon\) and \(\mu\) are uniform throughout the space.
  • Isotropic Medium: A medium where properties are the same in all directions at a given point.

questions.question: A uniform plane wave in the free space is normally incident on an infinitely thick dielectric slab (dielectric constant \(\varepsilon_r = 9\)). The magnitude of the reflection coefficient is
questions.explanation: The reflection coefficient \(\Gamma\) for a wave normally incident from a medium with dielectric constant \(\epsilon_{r1}\) to a medium with dielectric constant \(\epsilon_{r2}\) is given by: \[\Gamma = \frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r1}} - \sqrt{\epsilon_{r2}}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r1}} + \sqrt{\epsilon_{r2}}}\] Given: \[\epsilon_{r1} = 1\] \[\epsilon_{r2} = 9\] Substituting the values: \[|\Gamma| = \left| \frac{\sqrt{1} - \sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{1} + \sqrt{9}} \right| = \left| \frac{1 - 3}{1 + 3} \right|\] \[|\Gamma| = \left| \frac{-2}{4} \right| = \frac{2}{4}\] \[|\Gamma| = 0.5\] \[\boxed{(C):0.5}\]

questions.question: One end of a lossless transmission line having the characteristic impedance of \(75\ \Omega\) and length of \(1\ \text{cm}\) is short-circuited. At \(3\ \text{GHz}\), the input impedance at the other end of the transmission line is
questions.explanation:
Given a short-circuited transmission line with physical length \(l = 1\,\text{cm}\) and operating frequency \(f = 3\,\text{GHz}\). 1. Calculate the wavelength (\(\lambda\)):
\[\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}}{3 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz}} = 0.1\,\text{m} = 10\,\text{cm}\] 2. Determine the nature of the line:
Since \(l = 1\,\text{cm}\) and \(\frac{\lambda}{4} = \frac{10\,\text{cm}}{4} = 2.5\,\text{cm}\), we observe that \(l < \frac{\lambda}{4}\). A short-circuited transmission line with length less than \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\) exhibits an inductive nature. 3. Input impedance (\(Z_{SC}\)):
The input impedance of a short-circuited line is given by: \[Z_{SC} = j Z_{o} \tan(\beta l)\] where \(\beta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). \[\beta l = \left( \frac{2\pi}{10\,\text{cm}} \right) \cdot (1\,\text{cm}) = \frac{\pi}{5}\,\text{rad} = 36^{\circ}\] \[Z_{SC} = j Z_{o} \tan(36^{\circ})\] \[Z_{SC} \approx j 0.726 Z_{o}\] \[\boxed{(D):Inductive}\]
Key points
  • Short-circuited lines are inductive when \(0 < l < \frac{\lambda}{4}\) and capacitive when \(\frac{\lambda}{4} < l < \frac{\lambda}{2}\).
  • At \(l = \frac{\lambda}{4}\), the short-circuited line acts as an open circuit (parallel resonance).

questions.question: In the design of a single mode step index optical fiber close to upper cut-off, the single-mode operation is not preserved if
options: radius as well as operating wavelength are halved.
radius as well as operating wavelength are doubled.
radius is halved and operating wavelength is doubled.
radius is doubled and operating wavelength is halved.
questions.explanation:
For a step-index optical fiber, the condition for single-mode operation is determined by the normalized frequency \(V\), which must be less than \(2.405\): \[V = \frac{2\pi a}{\lambda} \text{NA} < 2.405\] where \(a\) is the core radius, \(\lambda\) is the operating wavelength, and \(\text{NA}\) is the numerical aperture. The single-mode operation is maintained if \(V < 2.405\). If \(V\) exceeds this value, multi-mode propagation occurs, meaning the single-mode operation is no longer preserved. Let us analyze option (d) where the radius \(a\) is doubled (\(a' = 2a\)) and the operating wavelength \(\lambda\) is halved (\(\lambda' = \frac{\lambda}{2}\)): \[V' = \frac{2\pi (2a)}{\frac{\lambda}{2}} \text{NA} = 4 \left( \frac{2\pi a}{\lambda} \text{NA} \right) = 4V\] Since the new normalized frequency \(V'\) is \(4\) times the original value, it is highly likely to exceed the cutoff limit of \(2.405\), thereby failing to preserve single-mode operation. \[\boxed{(D):\text {radius is doubled and operating wavelength is halved.}}\]
Key points
  • The normalized frequency \(V\) is directly proportional to the core radius \(a\) and inversely proportional to the operating wavelength \(\lambda\).
  • Single-mode fiber cutoff condition: \(V \leq 2.405\).
  • Increasing the core radius or decreasing the operating wavelength increases the number of modes supported by the fiber.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Confusing the relationship between \(V\) and \(\lambda\); \(V\) is inversely proportional to \(\lambda\), so decreasing \(\lambda\) increases \(V\).
  • Assuming all parameter changes affect \(V\) equally.

questions.question: A rectangular waveguide of internal dimensions (\(a = 4 \text{ cm}\) and \(b = 3 \text{ cm}\)) is to be operated in \(\text{TE}_{11}\) mode. The minimum operating frequency is
questions.explanation: The formula for the cutoff frequency \(f_{c}\) (labeled as \(f_{0}\) in the source) for a rectangular waveguide operating in the \(\text{TE}_{mn}\) mode is: \[f_{c} = \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^2}\] Given the dimensions \(a = 0.04\,\text{m}\), \(b = 0.03\,\text{m}\), and the speed of light \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\), for the \(\text{TE}_{11}\) mode (\(m=1, n=1\)): \[f_{c} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{0.04}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{0.03}\right)^2}\] Calculating the components within the square root: \[f_{c} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2} \sqrt{(25)^2 + (33.33)^2} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2} \times \sqrt{625 + 1111.11} \approx 6.25\,\text{GHz}\] \[\boxed{(A):6.25\,\text{GHz}}\]

questions.question: At \(20 \text{ GHz}\), the gain of a parabolic dish antenna of \(1 \text{ meter}\) diameter and \(70\%\) efficiency is
questions.explanation: The gain \(G\) of an aperture antenna (such as a parabolic reflector) can be calculated using its physical area \(A = \pi R^2\) and aperture efficiency \(\eta\). The formula relating gain to aperture efficiency and diameter \(D\) is: \[G = \eta \left( \frac{\pi D}{\lambda} \right)^2 = \eta \pi^2 \left( \frac{D}{\lambda} \right)^2\] Given the diameter \(D = 1\,\text{m}\), frequency \(f = 20\,\text{GHz} = 20 \times 10^9\,\text{Hz}\), and assuming standard efficiency \(\eta = 0.7\), we first calculate wavelength \(\lambda\): \[\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}}{20 \times 10^9\,\text{Hz}} = 0.015\,\text{m}\] Substituting the values into the gain formula: \[G = 0.7 \pi^2 \left( \frac{1}{0.015} \right)^2 \approx 30705.4359\] To convert the numerical gain into decibels: \[G(\text{dB}) = 10 \log_{10} (30705.4359) \approx 44.87 \approx 45\,\text{dB}\] \[\boxed{(D):45\text{ dB}}\]

questions.question: For a Hertz dipole antenna, the Half Power Beam Width (HPBW) in the E-plane is
questions.explanation: The electric field \(E\) for a Hertzian dipole in the \(E\)-plane (vertical plane or \(\theta\)-plane) is given by: \[E \propto \sin\theta\] The maximum electric field \(E_{\text{max}}\) occurs when \(\theta = 90^\circ\): \[E_{\text{max}} = E_0 \sin(90^\circ) = E_0\] The half-power points occur when the power density is half of its maximum value. Since power density is proportional to the square of the electric field (\(P \propto E^2\)), the electric field at the half-power points is \(1/\sqrt{2}\) times the maximum electric field: \[E = \frac{E_{\text{max}}}{\sqrt{2}}\] \[E_0 \sin\theta = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\] \[\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \implies \theta = 45^\circ, 135^\circ\] The Half-Power Beamwidth (HPBW) in the \(\theta\)-plane is the difference between these two angles: \[\text{HPBW} = 135^\circ - 45^\circ = 90^\circ\] \[\boxed{(C):90^\circ}\]
